edges.description: Loss of NDRG1- and periaxin-dependent Schwann-cell function impairs myelin maintenance and axon-glia interaction, producing demyelination with secondary axonal loss.

A block in Schwann-cell differentiation leaves the axon without a competent myelinating partner, reaching the compartment's shared terminal node by hypomyelination rather than by demyelination of formed myelin.

edges.description: CMT4H is a demyelinating neuropathy, and the reported functional defect is reduced Cdc42-dependent actin protrusion in Schwann cells and motoneurons. The steps between that cytoskeletal defect and demyelination are not established in the reporting study.

The Fig4 mutant mouse sciatic nerve shows reduced numbers of large-diameter myelinated axons with slowed conduction and reduced compound muscle action potential amplitude, the model correlate of this entry's terminal node. The steps from endolysosomal dysfunction to that nerve pathology are not established.

nodes.description: The shared terminal node of the autosomal-recessive CMT4 compartment. The diverse Schwann-cell and neuronal lesions (GDAP1 mitochondrial dysfunction, myotubularin phosphoinositide dysregulation, SH3TC2 trafficking defect, NDRG1 and periaxin loss, the EGR2 differentiation block, the frabin actin-remodelling defect, and the FIG4 endolysosomal defect) converge on demyelination — often with redundant myelin outfoldings or onion-bulb formation — and, over time, length-dependent secondary axonal degeneration. It is this secondary axonal loss, affecting the longest motor and sensory fibers first, that produces the progressive distal clinical deficit shared across all CMT compartments, typically with earlier onset and greater severity in the recessive forms. HK1 (CMT4G) is deliberately not linked to this or any other node: the CMT4G founder variant's functional effect is explicitly unresolved, so what is established for that subtype is an early-onset demyelinating neuropathy, not a mechanism through which the gene acts.

nodes.description: The CMT4E route. EGR2 is a transcription factor whose stable expression is specifically associated with the onset of peripheral myelination, and Egr2 null mice show a block of Schwann-cell differentiation at an early stage. Recessive EGR2 missense mutation in humans produces congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, a hypomyelinating rather than a demyelinating presentation. Note that the mouse evidence is from a null allele while the human CMT4E allele is missense, so the severity of the differentiation block in patients is an extrapolation, and this node records the program as abnormal rather than abolished.

nodes.description: The CMT4J route, and the reason FIG4 was previously the one CMT4 gene in this entry that reached no mechanism node. FIG4 is a phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate 5-phosphatase. Fibroblasts from the Fig4 mutant pale tremor mouse carry an abnormal concentration of PtdIns(3,5)P2 and a cytoplasm filled with large LAMP-2-immunoreactive vacuoles, which the authors read as dysfunction of the late endosome-lysosome axis. FIG4 is a second phosphoinositide lesion in this compartment, alongside the myotubularin lesion of CMT4B1 and CMT4B2, but the pathology reported for it is vacuolar rather than the myelin outfolding that characterizes CMT4B.

nodes.description: The CMT4H route. FGD4 encodes frabin, a GDP/GTP nucleotide exchange factor specific to Cdc42, a Rho-family GTPase. Truncated FRABIN mutants expressed in rat primary motoneurons and rat Schwann cells induce significantly fewer microspikes than wild-type protein, placing the lesion in Cdc42-dependent actin remodelling in the myelinating cell rather than in myelin protein structure or in membrane trafficking.

nodes.description: Biallelic GDAP1 mutations (CMT4A) disrupt regulation of the mitochondrial network. GDAP1 promotes mitochondrial fission, and its loss impairs mitochondrial dynamics in Schwann cells and neurons, producing a neuropathy that can be axonal, demyelinating, or mixed and is frequently accompanied by vocal cord paresis.

nodes.description: Biallelic loss of Schwann-cell genes NDRG1 (CMT4D / HMSN-Lom) and PRX / periaxin (CMT4F) disrupts myelinating Schwann-cell function and the axon-glia interaction required to maintain the myelin sheath. NDRG1 loss produces Schwann-cell dysfunction with early axonal involvement, and periaxin loss destabilizes the myelin sheath, in both cases yielding a demyelinating neuropathy.
